extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in anthropology, social evolution, and early human societies
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-style treatment of the character, habits, religions, and social organization of pre-historic men, arguing how those features conditioned the rise of civilisation. It synthesises anthropological observations (flint tools, descent rules, superstition) into general claims about early societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-historic man similar to modern savages in great characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not necessarily identical to the modern 'primitive man', pre-historic man shared the broad characteristics of present savages in morals, intellectual attainments, and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues we may reasonably imagine pre-historic man to be 'substantially a savage like present savages' on broad grounds, while allowing differences in acquired habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-historic man lacked ingrained superstitions and fixed bad habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-historic minds were likely not 'tattooed over with monstrous images' as modern savages are; the creation of habits, superstitions, and prejudices took ages and had not yet deeply fixed pre-historic minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This soft, impressible nature made primitive men more capable of acquiring civilised habits than modern savages; the distinction is between nature (similar) and acquisition (different).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remnant animal instincts could exist but wane under reason
rubrics_metrics.description: If early men were developed from animals they may initially have had animal instincts which gradually waned as reason grew; certain innate faculties can be reduced by learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: arithmetical prodigies lose their innate faculty when taught formal methods; similarly, 'irrational' instincts could be weakened by the growth of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simple flint tools indicates absence of valuable instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of flint tools—exactly those used by very poor people—suggests pre-historic men did not have valuable instincts that would have rendered such rudimentary tools unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: a race with useful instincts would either manage without such tools or make better ones; the regular improvement of tools mirrors transitions seen among modern savages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female-line descent (maternity-only) indicates moral licence in pre-historic societies
rubrics_metrics.description: The widespread reckoning of descent through the female only in prehistoric times is presented as evidence of an age of 'much licence' and weaker familial morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because paternity was legally unascertained, family cohesion and paternal authority were weak; this correlates with observations among lowest savages and slave-owning communities historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of paterfamilias (paternity recognition) undermines national/military cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where descent is traced through the mother, property and authority do not flow from father to children, producing 'ill-knit' groups less capable of forming disciplined, militarily effective nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Roman patria potestas and domestic despotism prepared citizens for military subjection; without such family discipline semi-moral nations would be easily conquered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason can weaken formerly beneficial instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: An instinct that began as a blind propensity can be diminished as reason develops, so races with reason but without certain instincts can outcompete those with instincts but without reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to sexual constancy or other traits: the loss of an instinct is possible and not necessarily disadvantageous when replaced by reason-driven behaviour or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-historic sexual morality was 'un-moral' rather than immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-historic people did not violate a conscience-based rule; rather, they lacked the developed conscience that would make sexual rules binding—thus they were 'un-moral.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed practices: strong men taking wives, repeated changes of partners, chastisement of wives—these indicate absence of conscience-based prohibitions rather than conscious transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savage religions are dominated by superstitions founded on luck and omens
rubrics_metrics.description: All savage religions are full of beliefs that casual omens, lucky places, animals, or actions portend good or ill, and savages typically cannot distinguish between a sign and a causative deity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay provides examples (sacred trees, lucky animals, healing springs) and analogies to gambling superstitions to illustrate the naturalness and ubiquity of omen-based beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single chance successes create durable superstitions (contagiousness and persistence of luck-beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single fortunate series of events or a socially-promoted claim can create a widely accepted charm or idol; such beliefs are easy to form and hard to eradicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'pretty fish' among boy gamblers; missionary cutting off a charm that then seemingly 'proves' its power when misfortune occurs; statistical refutation is often impractical for savages.

rubrics_metrics.name: A religion full of omens is a military and strategic disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations governed by omen-superstition are liable to panic, delay, or misdirected action (e.g., over-eclipse panic); this unpredictability is a liability in conflict with less superstitious foes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical such incidents show how reliance on auspices and omens undermines consistent military policy; thus universality of omen-beliefs indicates pre-historic religions resembled savage religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom-making power (authority enforcing fixed rules) is a prerequisite to civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early societies needed an authority capable of enforcing fixed rules of life to create calculable futures and make deferred enjoyment rational—this 'custom-making power' was the first thing in early society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although early authorities lacked conscious motives like protecting property, their effect was to generate stable practices that enabled civilisation's later development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate liability and contagious belief in luck enforce customs more than notions of desert
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that an action by one affects the whole tribe ('corporate liability') makes communities enforce customs strongly because any breach is thought to endanger all, not just the offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: fear of 13 at dinner, tribal prohibitions about eating animals of certain colours; such beliefs make inherited or traditional rules particularly binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs acquire force when presented as traditional or of remote antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities find rules more binding when they can be framed as traditional, ancient, or inherited, even if the rule actually derives from recent practical decisions (e.g., water distribution rules in Indian villages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities often present new arrangements as ancient in origin to secure acceptance; the essay cites Sir Henry Maine on the fiction of remote antiquity used to legitimise novel rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early social organisation: gregarious family groups under leaders and frequent migrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-historic societies likely existed in groups connected on the mother's side, gregarious under a leader, with frequent migrations that quickly produced dialectical and custom divergences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because migration was permanent and communication weak, descended groups developed new customs and languages rapidly, aiding the formation of distinct societies and 'luck' systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest, mixture, and conflict as regenerators of society and drivers of civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Incessant wars and the mixing of peoples through conquest fracture old images, infuse new elements, and act as the primary regenerators of society; modest superiority in conquerors facilitates civilising influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes the English experience in India as an example where too great a civilisational gap limits influence, whereas smaller differences allow conquerors to improve the conquered more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earliest property law prioritised common family property over individual private property
rubrics_metrics.description: Early jurisprudence concerned common family property rather than separate individual property; private property was small or nominal and the head of the family had plenary power over members' lives and goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal/social arrangement influenced early social aims and explains why customs and collective liabilities dominated early law rather than individual protections.
